html:
The revival of Hebrew turned a language used for prayer and study, but no one's mother tongue for nearly two thousand years, into the everyday language of millions. It began in Palestine in the late 1800s.

Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, who arrived in Jerusalem in 1881, insisted on speaking only Hebrew at home, raised his son as its first native speaker in modern times, and coined words for his great dictionary. The decisive step came in the schools and farming villages of the new immigrants, where children learned it as their first language. Teachers won a fight in 1913 to make Hebrew, not German, the language of the Technion.

Under the British mandate it was an official language from 1922. Today it is the main language of Israel. See also Zionism and the Hebrew alphabet.
